Multiple imputed data As a second sensitivity analysis, multiple imputation was conducted using the mice package in R, generating 20 imputed datasets via chained equations, receiving n = 166. For each imputed dataset, the same multilevel models were estimated using REML. Parameter estimates were then pooled across the 20 imputations using Rubin's rules, and standard errors and 95% CIs were derived from the pooled estimates as implemented in the mice package. The number of imputations used exceeds the minimum recommended to obtain stable estimates and adequately reflect sampling variability due to missing data (Rubin, 1987; White et al., 2011; van Buuren, 2018). Because Rubin's rules combine within-and between-imputation variability, additional bootstrap procedures were not applied. Variance components (class-and residual-level variance), ICCs, and variance reduction indices were calculated separately for each imputed dataset and then averaged across imputations to obtain pooled model-level statistics.

Results based on the multiply imputed datasets were highly consistent with the primary analyses. In Model 1, a one standard deviation increase in intellectual helplessness was associated with 0.29 SD increase in MA. Gender, age, and math achievement were not significant predictors. After adding general and test anxiety in Model 2, test anxiety emerged as a significant positive predictor, such that a one standard deviation increase corresponded to a 0.25 SD increase in MA, while general anxiety was not significantly related to MA.

Intellectual helplessness remained positively associated with MA, although the effect size was reduced (0.15 SD per one SD increase). In Model 3, which additionally included fluid intelligence and verbal working memory, test anxiety (0.22 SD increase in MA per one SD increase) and intellectual helplessness (0.17 SD increase) remained significant predictors. Fluid intelligence showed a negative association with MA, such that a one standard deviation increase corresponded to 0.12 SD decrease in MA, whereas verbal working memory was not significantly associated with MA. Model Comparison Using Maximum Likelihood

The four models reported in the main analyses were estimated using restricted maximum likelihood (REML). Because REML log-likelihoods are not comparable across models that differ in their fixed-effect structure, we re-estimated all models using full maximum likelihood (ML; REML = FALSE in lmer), which yields directly comparable log-likelihoods and thus permits formal model comparisons. Likelihood ratio tests (LRT) and information criteria (AIC and BIC) are valid only when all compared models are fitted to the same observations. Because of item-level missingness, the four main models in the main analyses were fitted to different samples (Model 1, n = 155; Model 2, n = 155; Model 3, n = 154; Model 4, n = 111). Therefore, here we conducted the model comparisons on the common completecase sample (n = 111), that is, the same subsample used for the complete-case sensitivity analysis (Table B).

The unconditional class model (M0) and Models 1 to 4 were re-estimated with ML on this sample and compared with sequential likelihood-ratio tests and with AIC and BIC; Akaike and Bayesian model weights were computed across Models 1 to 4. For reference, marginal R² is also reported. Because the class-level variance was estimated at zero in every conditional model, the random-effect variance could not be partitioned and conditional R² was undefined; the reported R² therefore reflects the fixed effects alone.

The models comparisons are presented in Table E. Adding the sociodemographic (gender, age) and math domain-specific (math achievement, intellectual helplessness in math) variables, together with school, to the unconditional model substantially improved model fit, χ 2 (11) = 62.46, p < .001.

Adding domain-general affective variables (general and test anxiety) further improved fit, χ 2 (2) = 8.15, p = .017. In contrast, adding domain-general cognitive variables (fluid intelligence and verbal working memory) did not improve fit, χ 2 (2) = 4.35, p = .114. Finally, adding family-related variables (mothers' home numeracy activities, mothers' MA, and mothers' education) did not improve fit either, χ 2 (3) = 0.35, p = .949. The information criteria converged with this pattern. AIC was lowest for Model 3 and, very similarily, Model 2 (229.75 and 230.10) and highest for Model 4 (235.40). The more conservative BIC was lowest for the parsimonious Models 1 and 2 (272.18 and 273.45) and penalized the more complex Models 3 and 4 (278.52 and 292.30). Expressed as model weights, Models 2 and 3 together carried 92% of the Akaike weight (.42 and .50), whereas the Bayesian weights concentrated on Models 1 and 2 (.64 and .34). Marginal R² rose from .596 (Model 1) to .625 (Model 2) and then changed only little (.639 in Model 3; .640 in Model 4); on the common sample the index is therefore essentially flat from the affective block onward, and the small apparent decline at Model 4 seen in Table B (and in Table 3 of the main text) reflects the different per-model samples used there rather than a genuine loss of fit.

Because Model 3 (with added domain-general cognitive block) does not involve the family variables, it could additionally be tested on the larger child-complete sample (n = 154), in which statistical power is greater. The domain-general cognitive block remained nonsignificant there, χ 2 (2) = 4.96, p = .084 (on that sample the preceding steps were χ 2 (11) = 80.68, p < .001 for the sociodemographic and math domain-specific block and χ 2 (2) = 17.19, p < .001 for the affective domain-general block). The non-significance of the domain-general cognitive block on the common sample is therefore not attributable solely to the reduced size of the n = 111 subsample.

Note that all of the conditional models (Models 1 to 4) were singular: the class-level variance was estimated at the boundary (approximately zero) once school was included as a fixed effect, consistent with the small ICCs reported in the main paper and in Table B. This does not affect the validity of the likelihood-ratio tests, because every compared model has the identical class random-effect structure, so the tests concern only the added fixed effects. Note also that, the comparison was conducted on the common complete-case sample so that all models are fitted to the same observations; the conclusions therefore apply to that subsample and are further supported by the larger-sample robustness check reported above.

Overall, the model comparison indicates that, beyond the domain-general affective block, the sequentially added domain-general cognitive and family blocks did not provide a statistically meaningful improvement in terms of model fit. This is consistent with the analytic aim of the present study, namely to assess the stability of the affective predictors under successive theory-driven controls rather than to maximize the variance explained in children's MA. This also mirrors the non-significant coefficients of the domain-general cognitive and family predictors reported in Table 3. The comparison presented here thus reinforces the conclusion that test anxiety is the central predictor of children's MA.

Across models, systematic differences between schools remained evident, whereas class-level variance was small (ICC = .019-.030). The proportion of variance in MA explained by fixed effects ranged from 58% to 62%, while the total variance explained by both fixed and random effects ranged from 59% to 63%. Relative to the unconditional class model estimated on the imputed sample, the inclusion of predictors reduced between-class variance by approximately 97-98%, while reductions in residual variance were moderate, approximately 24-31%.
